scams.name: Melbourne Airport Fake Taxi / DiDi Bait Scam
scams.description: You've landed at Tullamarine at 10pm with a sleeping toddler and two suitcases. A man in a high-vis vest at baggage claim says he can take you to the CBD 'cheaper than Uber, no waiting.' He walks you to the short-term carpark to an unmarked sedan. The ride runs for 40 minutes with no visible meter; at your hotel he demands $185. The Uber estimate on the same route was $55.
scams.avoidance: Your defence starts in the terminal. Walk past anyone offering transport inside the building — legitimate rideshare and taxi are only accessed outside, at signposted ranks or pickup bays. If you've booked Uber/DiDi, verify the licence plate and driver photo in-app before getting in, and watch for the 'code entry' — in fake-Uber scams, the scammer asks for a code but can't verify it. If you get into a taxi, make the driver uncover the meter before you pull away. The legitimate CBD fare from Tullamarine is approximately $60–$80 depending on time of day; anything over $100 is a scam. SkyBus ($22 one-way, every 10 minutes) is the tourist-proof alternative. Ignore all in-terminal transport offers — walk outside to the signposted ranks and rideshare bays; Verify driver photo and licence plate in the Uber/DiDi/Bolt app before entering the car; Take SkyBus ($22, runs every 10 min to Southern Cross Station) if in any doubt; Make the driver uncover the meter before pulling away — 'turn the meter on' is your first words; Pay with card on the in-car terminal for chargeback protection — never hand cash to an unmarked driver
scams.location: Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine), T2 and T4 arrivals, and the prepaid taxi/rideshare rank

scams.name: SIXT / Budget Phantom Rental-Car Damage Claim
scams.description: You return your rental SUV at Melbourne Airport with a clean walk-around from the desk agent. Two weeks later your credit card is charged AUD $1,040 for a 'scratch near the rear wheel' you never caused. The company sends a photo of damage that could have been there for months. Your email protest is met with a generic 'refer to T&Cs' reply.
scams.avoidance: Your defence is aggressive documentation. Before you drive off the lot, walk the entire car with your phone's video rolling — all four sides, roof, undercarriage (just drop the camera and film underneath), interior, odometer reading, fuel level, dashboard warning lights. Repeat at drop-off with the desk agent present on camera and ask them to verbally confirm 'no damage' on video. Pay with a credit card that offers CDW cover (Amex Platinum, Chase Sapphire), and keep all emails and video for 90 days after the trip. If a phantom charge appears, contest it with Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au) and your credit card's chargeback team — many travelers report the fee being reversed when challenged with video evidence. Film the entire car on video at both pickup AND drop-off — all sides, underneath, interior, dashboard; Insist on a signed no-damage receipt at drop-off with the desk agent present — photograph it; Pay with a credit card that provides primary CDW insurance (Amex Platinum, Chase Sapphire, Capital One Venture X); Decline rental-desk CDW upsells if your card covers it — keep the rental cost transparent; If hit with a phantom charge, file a chargeback immediately and complain to Consumer Affairs Victoria
scams.location: Melbourne Airport and CBD rental pickup counters — SIXT is the most-reported, but not the only

scams.name: Fake QR-Code Parking Ticket Sticker Scam
scams.description: You come back to your rental car on Swanston Street to find what looks like a parking infringement on the windshield — a yellow sticker with a 'City of Melbourne' logo and a prominent QR code saying 'Scan to pay $89 fine now or risk 25% late fee.' Stressed, you scan. The page loads, looks vaguely official, and takes your card details. The real scam is now live.
scams.avoidance: The fix is to never trust a QR code on a parking meter or windshield. Real Melbourne parking fines are issued by City of Melbourne or the local council, carry a numbered infringement notice, and are paid online at melbourne.vic.gov.au/parkingfines — you type that URL manually. Real parking meter payment is through the PayStay or CellOPark app, which you download from your phone's app store, not via any QR code on the physical meter. If you've already scanned a suspicious QR and entered card details, call your bank now, freeze the card and reissue. Never scan a QR code on a parking ticket or meter — type melbourne.vic.gov.au manually; Pay for parking only through the PayStay or CellOPark app downloaded from your app store; If you find a 'ticket', verify it by calling City of Melbourne (03 9658 9658) before paying; Photograph any suspicious sticker and report to City of Melbourne rangers for removal; If you've entered card details into a suspicious page, call your bank immediately and reissue
scams.location: CBD street-side parking, Southbank car parks, Carlton and Fitzroy metered zones

scams.name: Fake Short-Stay Rental / 'Airbnb' Scam
scams.description: You found a 'harbour-view apartment in Docklands' on a beautifully designed rental site — $140/night, photos of a Yarra River balcony, the host explains that Airbnb's fees are a ripoff and requests bank transfer. You send $980 AUD for a week. When you land at Tullamarine, the host's number is disconnected and the 'apartment' is someone's residential property that has never been listed for rent.
scams.avoidance: Your defence is identical to Sydney's: book only through the official Airbnb or Booking.com apps, bookmarked URLs, or a Google search result that lands on the real domain. Never click a link in an email or DM claiming to be a booking. Never pay by bank transfer, Western Union, Zelle or crypto — legitimate platforms escrow payment and don't release funds until after check-in. Reverse image-search the photos (drag into Google Images) — most fake listings reuse real estate marketing shots that are easy to find elsewhere. Ask for a live 60-second video call to confirm the property matches before paying. Book only through airbnb.com or booking.com via the app or a bookmarked URL; Never pay by bank transfer, wire or crypto — legitimate platforms always escrow; Reverse image-search the listing photos in Google Images before paying; Check the listing has reviews from multiple guests in the past 12 months; Ask for a live video call tour of the property — refusal is a hard no
scams.location: CBD, Docklands, Southbank, St Kilda — high-turnover short-stay areas

scams.name: Flinders Street / CBD Tram Pickpocket & Tab Bait
scams.description: You're standing in a rush-hour crowd at Flinders Street Station, phone out checking the next tram. Someone bumps your shoulder, apologises, and moves on. Three minutes later you reach for your phone to check the map and it's gone from your back pocket. You never felt the lift.
scams.avoidance: The related scam to watch for on the free City Circle tram and at rooftop bars near the CBD is 'tab inflation' — where the card reader appears to tap multiple times, the bill at end of night has an extra round you didn't order, or a 'system error' 5% surcharge appears. One traveler put it memorably: 'Strange how these places always only ever manage to overcharge, the system error is never in the customer's favour.' Your defence is keep your phone in a zipped front pocket, never the back, and scrutinise every bar bill before signing anything. Keep phone and wallet in a zipped front pocket, not a back pocket — obvious but chronic offence; Carry a slim crossbody bag across your chest, not a backpack on your back, on trams 70/75/96; Scrutinise every bar bill before signing — dispute any extra items or surcharges immediately; Tap your own card — never hand it to the staff to 'process' at the till; Use contactless or Myki for trams so your phone doesn't come out in crowded zones
scams.location: Flinders Street Station, Federation Square, trams 70/75/96, Elizabeth Street

scams.name: Great Ocean Road 'Day Tour' Fake Booking Scam
scams.description: You find a Great Ocean Road full-day tour with incredible reviews on a slick site — $65 per person, pickup from your Melbourne hotel. You book, receive a confirmation PDF that looks real. On tour day, no bus arrives. The phone number is dead. The 'operator' had no relationship to any legitimate Victorian tour company.
scams.avoidance: The safe pattern is to book through established operators with physical Melbourne offices: Gray Line Melbourne (grayline.com/melbourne), Go West Tours (gowest.com.au), Autopia Tours (autopiatours.com.au), or through a TripAdvisor/Viator/GetYourGuide booking with clear cancellation policy. Check Australian Business Number (ABN) registration at abn.business.gov.au — legitimate tour operators have public ABNs. Never pay by bank transfer for a tour; always use credit card for chargeback protection. If the tour doesn't show up, you'll be glad you can dispute the charge. Book through Gray Line, Go West, Autopia Tours, Bunyip Tours, or a verified Viator/GetYourGuide listing; Verify the operator's ABN at abn.business.gov.au — legitimate tours are ABN-registered; Pay only by credit card for chargeback protection — never bank transfer or PayPal F&F; Read TripAdvisor reviews from the last 6 months specifically — a gap suggests a new/fake listing; If no bus arrives, call the operator's landline first, then dispute the charge with your bank
scams.location: Online booking sites + Southern Cross Station pickup zone
